title: 1 Samuel 24:1–7
context: Saul resumes the hunt with three thousand men near En Gedi and enters a cave where David and his men are hiding. David’s men urge him to seize the moment, but he only cuts off a corner of Saul’s robe and is then troubled even by that. He restrains his men and lets Saul go. (In the Hebrew text these verses are numbered 24:2-8.)

verses.text: When Saul had returned from following the Philistines, he was told, “Behold, David is in the wilderness of En Gedi.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul returns from fighting the Philistines and immediately hears that David is at En Gedi. Arminian readers note how quickly he resumes the hunt, showing that the deliverance at Maon did not soften his heart.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Saul’s persistence as a mark of hardening. Even after God’s intervention turned him back, he takes up the chase again without any sign of reflection on what had happened.

verses.text: Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel, and went to seek David and his men on the rocks of the wild goats.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul takes three thousand chosen men to seek David on the rocks of the wild goats. Arminian readers see overwhelming odds that make David’s coming restraint all the more remarkable as a free and costly choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the contrast between Saul’s elite force and David’s small band of fugitives. The imbalance highlights that David’s survival depends on God rather than on military strength.

verses.text: He came to the sheep pens by the way, where there was a cave; and Saul went in to relieve himself. Now David and his men were staying in the innermost parts of the cave.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul enters a cave to relieve himself, unaware that David and his men are inside. Arminian readers see the vulnerability of the king and the moral test it creates for David.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see providence placing Saul in David’s power. The question is not whether God has arranged the moment but what David will do with it. Psalms 57 and 142 are linked by their headings to David in a cave, though which cave is not specified.

verses.text: David’s men said to him, “Behold, the day of which the LORD said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you.’ ” Then David arose and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe secretly.
verses.arminianNotes: David’s men say this is the day the LORD promised to deliver his enemy into his hand. No such word is recorded earlier in the book. Arminian readers note the temptation to read opportunity as divine permission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the men interpreting providence without God’s word, as Saul did at Keilah (23:7). David cuts off the corner of Saul’s robe, a symbolic act that recalls Samuel’s torn robe in 15:27-28.

verses.text: Afterward, David’s heart struck him because he had cut off Saul’s skirt.
verses.arminianNotes: David’s heart struck him because he had cut off Saul’s skirt. Arminian readers see a tender conscience responding to God’s Spirit, convicting David even of a small act of disrespect.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that conscience shaped by God’s word recognizes sin even in small things. David’s remorse shows reverence for God’s appointed king, even when that king is acting unjustly toward him.

verses.text: He said to his men, “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed.”
verses.arminianNotes: David refuses to harm the LORD’s anointed. Arminian readers see free restraint and trust in God’s timing rather than grasping at what was promised, a choice made in the face of strong pressure from his men.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David respecting God’s authority in Saul’s office, even though Saul has failed. The kingdom must come by God’s hand and in God’s time, not by David’s sword in a dark cave.

verses.text: So David checked his men with these words, and didn’t allow them to rise against Saul. Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on his way.
verses.arminianNotes: David restrains his men, and Saul leaves unharmed. Arminian readers note the moral leadership required to hold back men who wanted vengeance, and David’s responsibility for what his followers do.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see David’s restraint as faith in action, trusting God to fulfill his promise without violence. Both traditions see this as shared ground: the kingdom is not seized.
